the model says the meaning changed: DEC-261 (cited by the requirement) says a rewritten test of an approved example counts as failing and holds the merge until its original body passes, but the new code drops that flag whenever a judge answers "no" with confidence of 0.8 or more.; filed as a question for the owner, to ask with the question tool: The requirement still matches what you said you want: every edit to an approved record, including a changed acceptance test, goes back through the judge. It also relies on your earlier decision that a rewritten or extended test of an approved example counts as failing, and holds the merge, until a run of its original body passes.

The new code changes that. When a test was changed, the judge is now asked whether the change was made just to make it pass. If the judge answers "no, it was a real change" with confidence of 0.8 or more, the flag is dropped and the rewritten test stops holding the merge, even though its original body was never re-run and shown to pass. Your decision does not allow this way out.

What's unclear is whether you wanted this. The code mentions a report (report-fba0ba92), so it may have been a deliberate answer to a problem someone raised. But the only message from you near this change is "keep going", which doesn't clearly ask for it. Because it may have been on purpose, I'm not sending it back as a plain mistake.

the model says the meaning changed: The added test asserts that a rewritten acceptance test with a regression is no longer a hidden regression once a judge answers "no", but SR-207 and EX-5 say it resolves only when the original test body passes again.; filed as a question for the owner, to ask with the question tool: What you want: any change to an approved record, including a changed acceptance test, goes back through the judge. When new intent contradicts older intent, you are asked.

What the requirement says: if an approved example's test is rewritten so that a regression now passes, it is a hidden regression. It stays a hidden regression and holds the merge until the original test passes again, or until you agree to change the example. Your earlier decision (DEC-261) says the same thing: a rewritten test of an approved example counts as failing until its original version passes. The requirement and your intent agree.

What changed: a new test lets a judge decide whether the test was rewritten "just to make it pass". If the judge says no, the hidden regression goes away, even though the original test never passed again. Under that rule, a test rewritten to expect add(1, 2) == -1 could pass without holding the merge or asking you. That goes against examples EX-1, EX-5 and EX-6 and against DEC-261.

What's unclear: the change is labelled as the fix for defect report report-fba0ba92, so it may have been wanted on purpose. But the turn I have is a merge hand-off message from another session, not something you said about this. I can't tell whether you asked for a judge to be able to clear a hidden regression.

the model says the meaning changed: The added test expects a judge's "no" answer to clear the hidden-regression flag with no pass of the original test body, but SR-207 says it resolves only when the test body that passed before passes again (EX-5, EX-6).; filed as a question for the owner, to ask with the question tool: The requirement still matches what you asked for. You said a changed acceptance test of an approved example goes back through the judge, and you decided (DEC-261) that a rewritten test holds the merge until its original version passes again. The requirement says the same thing: a hidden regression clears only when the test that passed before passes again, or when you agree to change the outcome.

The new test adds a different way out. A judge reads the test change. If the judge says the test was not changed just to make it pass, the hidden-regression flag goes away, even though the original test never passed again and you were never asked. A test rewritten only to pass is still caught, so the add/subtract example (EX-1) still behaves as before. But a regression can now clear on the judge's word alone, which goes against EX-5 and EX-6.

The change came from a defect report (report-fba0ba92). The message logged before the edit is another agent's batch-landing summary, not your words, and it doesn't mention this change. It may be a deliberate improvement you'd want, or it may weaken a safeguard you chose. I can't tell which, so it's your call.

the model says the meaning changed: The new judge filter drops a hidden regression when a judge confidently calls the test change real, but the requirement says it resolves only when the original passing test body passes again.; filed as a question for the owner, to ask with the question tool: What you asked for: when an approved example's test is rewritten or extended, a person has to check that change. Separately, you only get asked when new intent conflicts with older intent. The requirement agrees with that. If a test that used to pass starts failing and the agent then rewrites the test so it passes, that's a "hidden regression". It stays flagged and holds the merge until the original test passes again. You confirmed this in an earlier decision. If the agent wants the example's outcome to change, you get asked. The change adds an AI check before a hidden regression is reported. If that check says with high confidence that the test was changed for a good reason and not just to make it pass, the flag disappears. Then the merge isn't held, you aren't asked, and the original test never has to pass again. That goes against the requirement and your earlier decision. What's unclear: the prompt from that turn was just "keep going", which didn't ask for this. But the code cites a report (report-fba0ba92), so it may have been a deliberate fix for false alarms. I can't tell whether you wanted it.
